p.src: This is how Sanshirō came to lend Yojirō money. The other night, at about nine o’clock, Yojirō suddenly arrived through the rain, saying at once that he was in serious trouble. Sanshirō looked at him and saw that his face was unusually pale. At first he thought it was because Yojirō had spent too long exposed to the cold air and autumn rain, but once he had sat down, Sanshirō saw that more than his complexion was amiss. He was uncharacteristically dejected. When Sanshirō asked, “Are you feeling unwell?” Yojirō blinked his deerlike eyes twice and replied: “The truth is, I’ve lost some money. I’m in a real fix.” He then assumed a slightly worried expression and sent two or three streams of tobacco smoke from his nostrils. Sanshirō could hardly remain silent and simply wait. As he gradually drew out what sort of money it was and where Yojirō had lost it, the matter soon became clear. Yojirō had held back only for as long as it took those two or three streams of smoke to leave his nose; after that, he smoothly related the whole story without the slightest difficulty. The money Yojirō had lost amounted to twenty yen—and it belonged to someone else. The previous year, when Professor Hirota rented his former house, he had been unable to raise the three months’ deposit and had temporarily borrowed the shortfall from Nonomiya. That money, however, was apparently something Nonomiya had specially asked his father back home to send because he needed to buy his younger sister a violin. Thus, while it was not needed that very day, the longer repayment was delayed, the more trouble it caused Yoshiko. Even now, Yoshiko was still making do without a violin. That was because Professor Hirota had not repaid the money. The professor would surely have repaid it long ago if he could, but he never had a penny left over each month and was a man who earned absolutely nothing beyond his salary, so the matter had simply been left as it was.

p.src: “I’m terribly sorry, because that’s the money I lost,” Yojirō said. He did indeed look thoroughly contrite. When Sanshirō asked where he had dropped it, Yojirō replied that he had not dropped it at all. He said he had bought several betting tickets and lost all the money. Even Sanshirō was utterly dumbfounded by this. The folly was so extreme that he did not even feel inclined to lecture him. Besides, Yojirō himself was utterly crestfallen. Compared with his usual exuberant vitality, it seemed there could only be two different Yojirōs. The contrast was too stark. The comedy and the pathos of it therefore swept over Sanshirō together. Sanshirō burst out laughing. At that, Yojirō began to laugh as well. “Oh, never mind. Something will turn up,” he said. “The professor doesn’t know yet?” Sanshirō asked. “Not yet.” “And Nonomiya?” “Of course he doesn’t know yet.” “When did you receive the money?” “At the beginning of this month, so it has been exactly two weeks today.” “When did you buy the tickets?” “The day after I received it.” “And you’ve left things like this from then until today?” “I’ve tried all sorts of ways to raise it, but I couldn’t, so there was nothing to be done. p.src: The campaign was making steady progress. Whenever he had a spare moment, he visited the lodging houses and consulted each student individually. Consultations had to be conducted one person at a time. When a crowd gathered, each man tried to assert his own importance and was liable to raise objections at the slightest opportunity. Otherwise, feeling that his presence had been ignored, he would adopt an aloof attitude from the outset. There was simply no way to consult people except one by one. It took time, of course. It cost money too. But no campaign could be carried on if one worried about such things. He also made a point of mentioning Professor Hirota's name as little as possible during these consultations. If people thought they were discussing the matter for Professor Hirota's sake rather than their own, nothing would ever be settled. This, it seemed, was how Yojirō was advancing the campaign. So far, everything had gone well. They had reached the point of agreeing that it would not do to have only Westerners and that a Japanese professor must be appointed. All that remained was to meet once more, choose a committee, and send it to the dean or the president to present their wishes. The meeting itself, however, would be a mere formality and could even be omitted. They already knew more or less which students would serve on the committee. They were all sympathetic to Professor Hirota, so depending on how the negotiations went, they might themselves put his name forward to the authorities. ...Listening to him, one might have thought that Yojirō alone could bend the whole world to his will. Sanshirō was greatly impressed by Yojirō's ability. Yojirō then began to justify having brought Haraguchi to the professor's house the other evening. “That evening, Haraguchi urged you to attend a gathering of literary men he was organizing, didn't he?” Yojirō said. Sanshirō remembered it, of course. According to Yojirō, that too had actually been his own idea.

p.src: Tonight in particular, there was no room for him to imagine himself at all. For some time now, Sanshirō had harbored doubts about Mineko. But merely doubting her got him nowhere. Yet there was not a single matter he could confront her with and demand an explanation for, so any clean, decisive resolution was out of the question. If some resolution was necessary for Sanshirō's peace of mind, all he could do was seize an opportunity to meet Mineko and, judging from her manner, deliver himself a more or less arbitrary final verdict. Tomorrow's meeting would provide indispensable evidence for that verdict. And so he imagined her in all sorts of ways. But however he imagined things, only scenes favorable to himself came to mind. Even so, the reality was highly doubtful. He felt as though he were gazing at a beautiful photograph taken of a filthy place. The photograph was unquestionably true as a photograph, yet the filthiness of the actual place was equally undeniable; the two things, which ought to have been identical, never coincided. At last, a cheering thought occurred to him. Mineko had said she would lend Yojirō the money. But she had also said she would not hand it to Yojirō. It was true that Yojirō might be a difficult man to trust where money was concerned. But whether that was really why Mineko would not give it to him was doubtful. If that was not the reason, it would be immensely encouraging for him. Her willingness simply to lend him the money was kindness enough. And her wish to meet him and place it directly in his hands meant—Sanshirō allowed his vanity to carry him this far, but then suddenly began to think, “Isn't she merely making a fool of me after all?” and abruptly flushed red. If someone had asked him why the woman would want to make a fool of him, Sanshirō would probably have been unable to answer.

If that was not the reason, it would be immensely encouraging for him.

p.src: Fortunately, two instructors were absent the next day, and the afternoon classes were canceled. Since returning to his lodgings seemed troublesome, he stopped along the way for a meal of à la carte dishes and then went to Mineko's house. He had passed the house any number of times. But this was his first time going inside. A nameplate reading “Kyōsuke Satomi” was displayed on a pillar of the tiled gate. Whenever Sanshirō passed this place, he wondered what sort of man Kyōsuke Satomi might be. He had never met him. The gate was closed. Entering through the small side door, he found the distance to the front entrance unexpectedly short. Rectangular slabs of granite had been laid at intervals. The front entrance was partitioned off by a fine, elegant lattice. He pressed the bell. When he said to the maid who answered, “Is Miss Mineko at home?” Sanshirō felt oddly self-conscious and embarrassed. He had never before stood at another person's front door and asked whether a young woman was at home. He found it exceedingly difficult to ask. The maid, contrary to his expectations, was perfectly serious. She was respectful as well. She went inside, returned, bowed politely, and invited him in; when he followed her up into the house, she showed him to the reception room. It was a Western-style room hung with heavy curtains. It was a little dark. The maid said once more, “Please wait a moment...” and withdrew. Sanshirō took a seat in the quiet room. Directly before him was a small fireplace recessed into the wall. Above it was a long horizontal mirror, with two candlesticks standing in front. Sanshirō looked at his face reflected between the candlesticks on either side, then sat down again. Then the sound of a violin came from somewhere deeper in the house. It vanished at once, as though the wind had carried it there from somewhere and then abandoned it. Sanshirō was sorry to lose it. Leaning against the deeply upholstered back of the chair, he listened intently, hoping the playing would continue a little longer, but the sound had ceased for good.

Considering how long she had kept him waiting, perhaps she had changed especially into something fine before coming into the drawing room. Now she sat there perfectly composed. As she watched Sanshirō in silence, a smile in her eyes and on her lips, he felt something more like a sweet torment. p.src: “If it doesn’t rain, perhaps I’ll go out for a little while,” she said, still standing by the window. Sanshirō took this to mean that she wanted him to leave. She had not changed into that lustrous silk kimono for his sake, either. “I’d better be going, then,” he said, rising to his feet. Mineko accompanied him to the entrance. As he stepped down onto the entryway floor and put on his shoes, Mineko said from above, “I’ll walk with you a little way. You don’t mind, do you?” “Yes, whichever you like,” Sanshirō replied as he tied his shoelaces. Before he knew it, she had stepped down onto the earthen floor. As she descended, she brought her lips close to Sanshirō’s ear and whispered, “Are you angry?” Just then the maid hurried out to see them off. The two walked side by side in silence for about half a block. All the while, Sanshirō was thinking about Mineko. She must have been brought up to have her own way. And at home she must enjoy more freedom than most women, doing everything exactly as she pleased. One could tell from the way she was walking through the streets with him now, without asking anyone’s permission. She could probably behave this way because she had no elderly parents and her young brother believed in leaving her to herself; but in the country it would surely cause no end of trouble. What would she do, he wondered, if she were told to live a life like Omitsu of Miwada? Tokyo was unlike the country: everything here was open and unrestricted, so perhaps most women in the capital were like this; yet when he had imagined them from afar, they had seemed rather more old-fashioned. Then it occurred to him that Yojirō had indeed been right to call Mineko an Ibsen woman. But was she Ibsen-like only in her disregard for social conventions, or did the thoughts in the depths of her heart follow Ibsen as well? That he could not tell. Before long they emerged onto Hongō Avenue.

Mineko stopped before one of them. “It must be Venice.” This much even Sanshirō could tell. Somehow, it did look like Venice. It made him feel that he would like to ride in a gondola. Sanshirō had learned the word “gondola” when he was in high school. Ever since then, he had liked the word. Whenever he thought of a gondola, he felt it simply had to be ridden in with a woman. Silently he gazed at the blue water, the tall houses on either side, their inverted reflections, and the flecks of red glimmering among the shadows. Then Mineko said, “The brother seems by far the better painter, doesn’t he?” Sanshirō did not understand what she meant. “The brother—?” “This painting is by the brother, isn’t it?” “Whose brother?” Mineko looked at Sanshirō with a puzzled expression. “But those over there are by the sister, and these here are by the brother, aren’t they?” Sanshirō stepped back and looked along one side of the way they had just come. Countless similar paintings of foreign scenery hung there. “Am I wrong?” “Did you think they were all by one person?” “Yes,” he said, looking blank. Presently their eyes met. p.src: “Miss Satomi!” someone suddenly called out in a loud voice. Mineko and Sanshirō both turned their heads. Haraguchi stood about six feet from an entrance marked “Office.” Behind him, partly obscured by his figure, stood Nonomiya. Rather than Haraguchi, who had called her, Mineko looked at Nonomiya farther behind him. The instant she saw him, she stepped back two or three paces and came to Sanshirō’s side. Without making the gesture noticeable, she brought her lips close to Sanshirō’s ear. Then she whispered something. Sanshirō could not make out a single word. Before he could ask her to repeat it, Mineko had gone back toward the two men. She was already exchanging greetings with them. Turning to Sanshirō, Nonomiya said, “You’ve come with an unusual companion.” Before Sanshirō could answer, Mineko said, “We suit each other, don’t we?” Nonomiya said nothing. He turned abruptly around. Behind him hung a large painting about the size of a tatami mat. It was a portrait. The entire painting was dark. The clothes and hat received so little light that they were indistinguishable from the background; only the face was white. The face was thin, its cheeks hollow. “It’s a copy, isn’t it?” Nonomiya said to Haraguchi. Haraguchi was now busily telling Mineko something. —The exhibition was nearly over. The number of visitors had fallen considerably. At the beginning of the exhibition he had come to the office every day, but lately he seldom showed his face. Today, for the first time in quite a while, he had business here and had dragged Nonomiya along. What a fortunate encounter this was. Once this exhibition closed, preparations for the next year’s had to begin at once, so he was extremely busy.

p.src: The woman turned and entered another room. The man followed one step behind her. It was a dark room with little light. Looking at the late Professor Fukami's paintings hung in a row along the long, narrow wall, he saw that, just as Haraguchi had pointed out, they were almost all watercolors. What struck Sanshirō most was how subduedly the watercolors were painted: every one used pale colors, few in number and lacking in contrast, so that they seemed unlikely to show to advantage unless brought out into the sunlight. Yet the brushwork showed not the slightest hesitation. They had the air of having been completed in a single sweep. The pencil outlines showed clearly through beneath the paint, and this too revealed the elegant nonchalance of his style. The human figures were thin and elongated, just like threshing flails. There was a painting of Venice here as well. “This is Venice too, isn't it?” the woman said, coming closer. “Yes,” he said, but Venice suddenly reminded him of something. “What did you say a moment ago?” The woman asked, “A moment ago?” she asked in return. “When I was standing there looking at that painting of Venice.” The woman once again showed her perfectly white teeth. But she said nothing. “If it wasn't anything important, I needn't ask.” “It wasn't important.” Sanshirō still looked puzzled. It was already past four on that overcast autumn day. The room was growing dim. There were very few visitors. In the other room there were only the shadows of a man and a woman. The woman left the paintings and stood directly before Sanshirō. “Nonomiya. You know—remember?” “Nonomiya...” “Now you understand, don't you?” Mineko's meaning flooded Sanshirō's heart all at once, like a great wave breaking over him. “Were you making a fool of Nonomiya?” “Why?” Her tone was entirely innocent. All at once, Sanshirō lost the courage to say anything more. Without a word, he began to move away, taking two or three steps.

p.src: “I wasn't making a fool of you.” Sanshirō stopped again. Sanshirō was a tall man. He looked down at Mineko from above. “Then that's all right.” “Why would it be wrong?” “That's why I say it's all right.” The woman turned her face away. They both walked toward the doorway. As they passed through the doorway, their shoulders touched. The man suddenly remembered the woman with whom he had shared a train carriage. The place where he had touched Mineko's flesh seemed to throb as it might in a dream. “Is it really all right?” Mineko asked in a low voice. A group of two or three visitors was coming toward them. “In any case, let's go outside,” Sanshirō said. They retrieved their footwear and went out, only to find that it was raining. “Shall we go to Seiyoken?” Mineko did not answer. Getting wet in the rain, they stood in the broad open ground before the museum. Fortunately, the rain had only just begun. Moreover, it was not heavy. Standing in the rain, the woman looked around and pointed toward the woods in the distance. “Let's shelter under those trees.” It looked as though the rain might stop if they waited a little. They took shelter beneath a large cedar. It was not a tree well suited to keeping off the rain. Yet neither of them moved. They remained standing there even as they got wet. They both grew cold. The woman said, “Ogawa.” The man, his brows drawn together, turned toward the woman the face that had been gazing up at the sky. “Was it wrong? What I did a moment ago.” “It's all right.” “But...” she said, moving closer. “For some reason, I simply wanted to do that. I didn't mean to be disrespectful to Nonomiya.” The woman fixed her eyes on Sanshirō. In her eyes Sanshirō perceived an appeal deeper than words. —After all, didn't I do it for your sake? the depths of her double-lidded eyes pleaded. Once more, Sanshirō answered, “That's why I say it's all right.” The rain grew steadily heavier.
